note: Coordinates from OpenStreetMap (via Mapcarta) and Wikipedia, checked against 0.6 m NAIP aerial photos. Room counts and dates are commonly cited figures; sources in the README.

sites.name: Pueblo Bonito
sites.note: The largest great house: a D-shaped building of four stories around two plazas, built in stages over almost three centuries.
sites.sky: A wall across the central plaza runs north–south almost exactly, so its shadow disappears at local noon, and the western half of the front wall runs east–west, toward the equinox sunrise and sunset.

sites.name: Chetro Ketl
sites.note: Second largest great house, with a great kiva in its plaza and a 13-column colonnade added after 1105, unlike anything else in Chaco.

sites.name: Pueblo del Arroyo
sites.note: Built beside Chaco Wash, with a rare tri-wall structure (three concentric walls) against its back.

sites.name: Kin Kletso
sites.note: A compact, late great house built in a few years, with a two-story round tower kiva.

sites.name: Casa Rinconada
sites.note: The largest excavated great kiva at Chaco, on the south side of the canyon. Excavated by Gordon Vivian in 1930–31 and heavily rebuilt afterwards.
sites.sky: Shortly after summer solstice sunrise, light through a window in the northeast wall falls on one of the wall niches. It's a popular story, but the upper wall and window were rebuilt after excavation, and a roof post would have blocked the beam, so it may not be original.

sites.name: Pueblo Alto
sites.note: On the mesa top north of the canyon, where the Great North Road begins. Huge trash mounds suggest gatherings and feasts.
sites.sky: The Great North Road leaves here about 15° east of north, then runs close to due north much of the way to Kutz Canyon, about 50 km away.

sites.name: Peñasco Blanco
sites.note: The westernmost great house, on the mesa above where Chaco Wash meets the Escavada.
sites.sky: Below it, on an overhang near the canyon trail, a red pictograph of a star, a crescent moon and a hand may record the supernova of July 1054, which appeared next to the crescent moon.

sites.name: Una Vida
sites.note: One of the three earliest great houses, with petroglyph panels on the cliff behind it.

sites.name: Hungo Pavi
sites.note: A great house that has never been excavated; its outline still shows as a rubble mound.

sites.name: Wijiji
sites.note: The last Chacoan great house built in the canyon: small, symmetrical and finished in a few years.

sites.name: Fajada Butte
sites.note: A 135 m butte at the south entrance to the canyon. Closed to visitors to protect the site.
sites.sky: Near the top, three leaning slabs throw daggers of light across two spiral petroglyphs: one pierces the large spiral at the summer solstice, two frame it at the winter solstice, and one crosses the small spiral at the equinoxes. Shadows from the rising Moon reach the spiral's edge at the major lunar standstill and its center at the minor one. Found by Anna Sofaer in 1977; one slab shifted in 1989 and the markings are no longer exact.
